extracted.intended_audience: ALSC / John Newbery Medal and other ALSC award committee members (children's literature award committee members)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and eligibility rules for members serving on the John Newbery Medal (and related ALSC award/media evaluation) committees, including conflict-of-interest, confidentiality, external communication rules, and detailed publication/eligibility definitions for candidate books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to write unsigned reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of all committees may write and publish unsigned reviews of any book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a permissible option for committee members to continue professional reviewing activity while minimizing conflict/appearance of influence; no further restrictions stated for unsigned reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted signed reviews / social media for non-U.S. works (general committees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of all committees (except the Batchelder) may write signed reviews or discuss via social media any book previously published in other countries or by an author or illustrator who is not an American citizen or resident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows signed bylines and social-media discussion about works that cannot be eligible for the committee’s consideration because of publication origin or author/illustrator non-U.S. residency/citizenship. Batchelder is the exception with its own rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batchelder committee signed-review exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Batchelder committee members may write signed reviews or discuss via social media any book that has not been translated and published in the United States in the previous year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a special-case permission tailored to Batchelder's focus on translated works; it permits signed public commentary on books that are clearly out of scope for the committee’s eligible pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee-specific permitted reading/discussion areas (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for committee members about genres/fields they may publicly review: e.g., 'Books with no illustration provide a wide field for members of the Caldecott committee'; 'Books with no text are available for Newbery committee members'; 'Belpré committee members may write signed reviews or discuss via social media any books by non-Latinx authors and illustrators'; 'Sibert committee members may write signed reviews or discuss via social media all works of fiction'; 'Geisel committee members may write signed reviews or discuss via social media any books beyond the scope of a beginning reader'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are illustrative options (from past-President LaTronica) showing which categories of books are safe for committee members to discuss publicly without risking conflict with eligibility; they are suggestions rather than exhaustive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on discussing eligible titles (electronic and print) during term
rubrics_metrics.description: Award committee members may not blog or otherwise communicate electronically (outside of the committee process) regarding any aspect of eligible titles during their term of service. At no time during or after their service may committee members discuss the status of books as having been or not having been a consideration, suggested, and/or nominated for the award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad confidentiality rule covers any electronic or print communication about eligible titles during the term, and extends to not discussing whether a title was considered or nominated even after service ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of service timing and resumption of reviewing activity
rubrics_metrics.description: ALSC policy indicates that you may not engage in print or electronic communication regarding eligible titles during your 'term of service,' which officially begins July 1 of your appointment year. If appointed after July 1, your term begins immediately. Once your committee’s selections have been announced at the LibLearnX Youth Media Awards Press Conference, you may resume bylined reviewing, writing articles, and blogging even though the term does not end until the following Annual Conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special note about galleys: the July 1 cut-off applies to books in galley form because official publication dates can shift. Between July 1 and when the committee’s year under consideration begins, members may review finished published books from prior years and imports that cannot be eligible. After January 1 you may review books published in the previous year. Example provided: a 2021 committee member could review any 2019 book in final form but not any galleys produced after July 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on writing teachers' or readers' group guides (advisory capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy does not permit members to write teachers’ guides or readers’ group guides for children’s trade-book publishers while serving on an award committee because that is considered serving in an advisory capacity to a trade publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to serve on an award committee, you must forgo writing these sorts of items during your term of committee service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary library reference assistance is not advisory capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing assistance as part of ordinary library reference duties (e.g., helping an author with research when called by the library) does not disqualify a member from serving on an award committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledgement in a book for routine reference help does not equal advisory service to a trade publisher; it is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of a dedication to a member is disqualifying
rubrics_metrics.description: If a children’s book is being dedicated to you that will come out during your term of service, you may not accept an appointment to the committee. If you learn of the dedication once your term begins, you are expected to resign as soon as you find out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dedication is treated as creating a conflict of interest or appearance thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close personal relationship / conflict-of-interest standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'close personal relationship' is defined as one that could reasonably be seen by an outsider as having an influence on your decision-making process. This includes close friends and co-workers; it does not include casual acquaintances (e.g., conference speakers, someone who sat next to you at a dinner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt about the degree of friendship, discuss specifics with the ALSC Executive Director. The intent is to avoid appearances like 'their best friend was on the committee.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting publishers' invitations to meals/social events
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers often invite committee members to be guests at meals and social gatherings at professional conferences; it is fine to accept such invitations as long as they do not conflict with committee meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should be vigilant about maintaining confidentiality in these gatherings and may wish to discuss other topics rather than books; be aware many will hang on your words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate family definition for conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: ALA’s attorneys advise that only parents, children, spouses, and partners must be included in the definition of 'immediate family.' Siblings and other relatives (cousins, etc.) fall outside this narrow definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrower legal definition is used because relationships with parents/children/spouses/partners are more susceptible to claims of conflict due to stronger emotional and direct financial ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing adult books does not disqualify committee service
rubrics_metrics.description: Members who are authors of adult books scheduled for publication during their committee term are not disqualified from serving on a children's award committee because adult books are ineligible for ALSC children's awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different rules apply to books that would be eligible for the committee in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscripts under consideration / under contract and committee service
rubrics_metrics.description: Members must avoid any appearance of conflict of interest. A manuscript under contract would infer a financial tie to a publishing house and could disqualify a member; if a manuscript is being considered by a publisher and there is a good chance it will be published in your year of service, you should decline appointment. If uncertain, contact the ALSC Executive Director to verify publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: critique given on a manuscript last year may be problematic if publication during service year is likely. The Chair or PGC (with ALSC staff) should verify questions about publication dates, not individual members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional books about children’s literature permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are not disqualified from serving if they write, edit, or contribute to a book about children’s literature that is aimed at professionals or other interested adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such publications are considered professional, not trade children's books, and thus do not create disqualifying conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for soliciting outside opinions (verbal/in-person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee members are strongly encouraged to speak with others—children and adults—regarding eligible books to learn a variety of perspectives, but must maintain confidentiality of committee proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When participating in verbal, in-person discussions members should: practice active listening; ask open-ended questions; share public information about the award process and terms/criteria; keep their own comments minimal, especially negative comments; use sensitivity and positive frameworks when discussing material they personally find weak; be careful not to publicly dismiss a book; try to avoid direct comparisons between two eligible titles and set context before discussion (e.g., remind participants you must consider all eligible titles); only express your own personal opinion and be clear you are not speaking for the committee (use 'I' rather than 'we').

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock award discussions (participation limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee members are allowed and encouraged to participate in local book discussions (especially with children) but must not participate in mock elections. A committee member may observe a mock discussion but should not discuss eligible titles or vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a member is required by employment to hold a mock election, they should discuss this with the Chair and PGC to find an acceptable approach that preserves confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality about past committee deliberations
rubrics_metrics.description: Members may not reveal details of committee decision-making from past service. They may discuss their own opinions of that year's books but not the opinions of other committee members or the internal decision-making process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This long-term secrecy protects the freedom of committee deliberation by ensuring members can speak candidly in committee without fear their remarks will be publicly disclosed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-year cooling-off period between service on certain committees
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a four-year waiting period between service on the Batchelder, Caldecott, Geisel, Newbery, Sibert, Legacy, or Notable Children’s Books Committees. The period begins from the last year of the term of service and follows the Olympic model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational exception: the four-year period may be suspended for emergency mid-year replacements to provide flexibility. Appointment to a Chair position may occur within the four-year period, but a prior Chair may not be appointed to a member position within the four years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the John Newbery Medal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Newbery Medal is established to encourage original and creative work in the field of books for children and to emphasize that contributions to the literature for children deserve recognition similar to that given to poetry, plays, or novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The award aims to encourage good writing for children and to honor librarians who promote children’s reading interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newbery recipient and nationality/residency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The medal is to be awarded annually to the author of the 'most distinguished contribution to American Literature for children' and the award is restricted to authors who are citizens or residents of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The award covers books whose publication falls in the calendar year last elapsed. Reprints and compilations are not eligible. The judgment of the librarians voting decides whether a book is a 'contribution to the literature for children.'

rubrics_metrics.name: American Literature for children — origin-based definition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'American Literature' refers to the origin of the book (author/publisher), not to the action's time or location, nor to characters or setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a book set in England can be eligible if the author is American and the publisher is U.S.-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original work requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The intent is to ensure that a book is a NEW creation and not a re-creation from some other work; no significant part of the book under consideration should have been originally part of another work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor portions previously published are allowed if the substantial majority of the book is new; when in doubt the Chair should consult the PGC and ALSC staff. Examples given (re-illustrated editions vs. entirely new illustrations; quotation/visual quotation cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Young readers' editions ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's books derived from previously published adult books, including young readers’ editions, are not eligible because the award is intended for original creation of a distinguished book for children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not exclude new works created from public-domain sources (e.g., novels based on Shakespeare plays). Example: a young readers’ edition that substantially repackages an adult book would be ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compilations/anthologies ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthologies and compilations of works by many authors are not eligible because they consist of multiple distinct elements and are not a unified whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a book of ten distinct short stories by different authors was ruled ineligible even if authors were U.S. residents because it is not a single work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portion previously published elsewhere — minor portion allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a portion of a book was previously published (e.g., magazine, short story), the amount previously published must be a minor portion of the entire work; the substantial majority must be wholly new and previously unpublished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: single-chapter previously published within a longer book was acceptable; substantially expanded versions of prior articles may be eligible if most content is new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional works / retellings permitted if original
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee may consider books that are traditional in origin if the book is the result of original research and the retelling and interpretation are the writer’s own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: retellings of folk tales or mythic material are eligible when the author creates an original retelling for children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous publication (definition and eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Published simultaneously' means a book was first published in the United States within the same calendar year that it was first published in any other country, whether or not the actual dates are identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: jointly acquired and jointly edited U.S./U.K. publication released within a few days of each other can be ruled eligible based on joint editorial work; if editorial work originated only in another country it would be ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: First published in the United States — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘First published in the United States’ means the acquisition of the book and the editorial work were done by a publisher with editorial offices in the United States that publishes under U.S. conventions for a U.S. market. A book may be eligible if published 'simultaneously' provided editorial work was done jointly or originated in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers with only U.S. warehouses/distribution but editorial offices elsewhere are excluded; editorial work must originate in a U.S. editorial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication date clarification rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally a book has a publication date in the award year, is available for purchase in that year, and has a copyright date no later than that year. If a book is published prior to its year of copyright, it shall be considered in its year of copyright; if published after its year of copyright, it should be considered in the year of its publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent is that every eligible book be considered but no book in more than one year. Publication dates may be determined from the book, publisher’s website, Library of Congress catalog, or other sources; verification by Chair/PCG and ALSC staff if needed, not by individual members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed (definition for eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed means transmitted from the publisher to the wholesale or retail seller and may (or may not) also include marketing and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to clarify whether a book is 'published' in the U.S. when considering eligibility; example: many small publishers use a distributor that handles distribution to retailers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial work (definition for eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Editorial work' means the negotiation process between author and editor that leads from initial manuscript to finished book; may include conversations, correspondence, written instructions, markings on drafts, or other communication about the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether editorial work was done in a U.S. editorial office can determine U.S. publication status for eligibility (see examples such as joint editorial work between countries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial office (definition for eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Editorial office' means where 'editorial work' is officially done (the business address at which such work originates); secondary/subsidiary offices are excluded. An office that only acquires manuscripts or distributes completed books is not considered an editorial office unless editing is also done there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: foreign publishers with a U.S. office used solely for facilitation are not considered U.S. publishers if editing is performed at the foreign headquarters.
